desc:
A terrain is a row of unit-width columns, heights[i] units tall. After a long rain, the water standing above column i is

water[i] = min(max(heights[0..i]), max(heights[i..n-1])) - heights[i]

(the usual trapped-water rule: the level is limited by the lower of the tallest column to the left and the tallest to the right, each including column i itself).

A pool is a maximal run of consecutive columns that each hold at least one unit of water. Return the volume of the largest pool (the sum of water[i] over its columns), or 0 if there is no water at all.

heights = [4, 1, 3, 0, 2, 5, 1, 0, 6]
water   = [0, 3, 1, 4, 2, 0, 4, 5, 0]
pools: columns 1..4 hold 10, columns 6..7 hold 9
result = 10
hints: First solve the usual question: how much water sits above each column? Prefix and suffix maxima give it in O(n) with extra arrays.
To avoid the two extra arrays, use two pointers with a running left maximum and a running right maximum: always process the side whose current column is lower.

Store (or directly accumulate) the water of every column. Walk through the columns once more: add to the current pool while water[i] > 0, and when a column with zero water appears, close the pool and compare it with the best so far.
editorial: Pools are separated exactly by columns with zero water, i.e. columns at least as tall as the water level around them. So the problem is the standard trapped-water computation followed by a scan for the best run of positive values.

Two pointers compute the water without prefix arrays. Keep lmax and rmax. If heights[l] < heights[r], the right side already has a wall at least as tall as heights[l], so the level above column l is decided by lmax alone: update lmax, set water[l] = lmax - heights[l] and advance. Otherwise do the mirror image on the right. The pointers meet at a column that is a global maximum, which holds no water.
The scan over water sums each run of positive entries and keeps the maximum. Total time O(n), space O(n) for the water array (it could be fused into the main loop with a little more care).
